args.topic: Tenant's notice of the landlord's noncompliance
Liquidated damages and early termination fees

content:
Whether you can leave over the AC and the mold, and skip the fee, is not settled yet. Here is each way out and where it stands.

1. Ending the lease because the repair was not made: not settled.
The rule: you may end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply" within 7 days after your written notice that names the problem and says you intend to end the lease over it (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). Your lease promises this repair: the landlord shall "maintain in good working order and repair the heating, air-conditioning" (Lease Section 7.1).
Applied: the duty is met, the problem was not caused by you, and you confirmed your notice named it and said you intend to end the lease. The program's deadlines show the 7 days have passed. Two points are open.
- Paying rent. The statute says a tenant who "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" waives ending the lease, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). You confirmed paying rent after you knew of the problem. The statute does not settle this. One reading: a problem still not fixed is a continuing noncompliance, so paying did not waive ending the lease. Other reading: the failure to fix the problem you already knew of is the noncompliance, so paying waived it, and only a new or different failure starts over. On the first reading this option is open. On the second it is closed.
- "Materially." The statute does not define it (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). One reading: a failure of a duty that 83.51(1) lists counts whatever its size. Other reading: it turns on degree, meaning how serious the condition is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living in the unit. You confirmed the AC is not a structure or plumbing item, and the tool does not hold local codes, so the first reading would turn on a code (see the second option). 83.56(1) also reaches "material provisions of the rental agreement," and your lease promises this repair. On the degree reading, the leak, the black spots, your asthma, and how long it has gone on weigh for you. The techs saying they need parts weighs the other way.
So: if the first reading of the rent point holds and the problem counts as material, you "may terminate the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)), and no step is left, since the notice and the 7 days are done. The statute does not mention a fee there. If the second reading holds, this way out is closed.
One more point: if the wait for parts is a cause beyond the landlord's control and the landlord "continues to make every reasonable effort," a different part of the statute applies. If the problem makes the unit untenantable and you vacate, "the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)(a)). Nothing you confirmed shows whether the parts delay fits that, so it is not known yet.

2. Not paying rent because of the problem: not known yet.
That defense reaches only a failure of a duty in 83.51(1), not a lease promise alone (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). You confirmed the problem is not structure or plumbing. So it turns on whether a building, housing, or health code where the unit is requires the landlord to fix it (Fla. Stat. 83.51(1)(a)). The tool does not hold those codes. The city or county code enforcement office can tell you, and can inspect the unit. If a code covers it, you would first need a new written notice that says you intend not to pay rent because of the problem, then 7 days (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). Your earlier notice said you intend to end the lease, not that you will stop paying. If the landlord then sued for possession and you raised the defense, you would have to pay rent into the court registry within "5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays" after service (Fla. Stat. 83.60(2)); the tool does not compute that date. If no code covers it, this option is closed. Moving out and simply stopping rent is not a way out the statute gives. If the lease is not ended, one choice the landlord has is "holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(3)).

3. Leaving early and paying the fee: not known yet.
Your lease lets you end it early with "at least sixty (60) days' written notice" and a fee of $1,578.00 (Lease Section 12.1), and says you may not end it early "except as provided in Article 12 or as required by law" (Lease Section 2.2). The statute allows an early termination fee only if you signed "a separate addendum to the rental agreement" when the lease was made, the amount is within two months' rent, and the notice required is "no more than 60 days" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tool found no addendum or liquidated damages term in your lease's text, and the sheet asks whether you signed one. If you did not, this route is closed under the statute. If you did, it turns next on the amount, which Lease Section 12.1 says "does not exceed two (2) months' Rent", and on the notice, where the lease says "at least" 60 days and the statute says "no more than" 60 days. You can check both against the addendum. The reassignment the manager mentioned is in the lease too: it needs the landlord's written approval and a "reassignment fee of $250.00" (Lease Section 11.1).
Your mom: your lease says your parent "shall sign a separate Guaranty of this Lease" (Lease Section 4.3). The tool has not read that guaranty, so what it covers is something you can check in that document.

4. Notice before you leave: not known yet.
If you vacate before the term ends, your lease asks for 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery, and says without it you "shall forfeit the security deposit" (Lease Section 9.2; Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). Whether that is still open turns on your planned move-out date, which the sheet asks. The servicemember way out is closed because you confirmed you are not a servicemember (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)).

What the cases say (all development-run pages, not yet verified by the author):
- K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith, 445 So. 2d 1032 (Fla. 5th DCA 1984), read the 1981 statute. Tenants who withheld rent over poor upkeep sued for the lost value of their apartments. The court said "it is necessary for the tenant to comply with section 83.56" (at 1037). You gave a written notice, so you are on the right side of that. It differs from yours in being a damages claim, and it does not say a notice ends the lease.
- Lakeway Management Co. of Florida v. Stolowilsky, 527 So. 2d 950 (Fla. 3d DCA 1988), read the 1985 statute. Tenants stopped paying rent and left a one-year lease. The court barred their constructive eviction defense because their first written complaint came only after the landlord's three-day notice: "a complaint in writing which would meet the condition precedent to urging constructive eviction" (at 951). Yours differs: you complained in writing first, and nothing confirmed shows a three-day notice. It cuts against anyone who leaves and stops paying with no earlier written notice.
- Olen Properties Corp. v. Moss, 984 So. 2d 558 (Fla. 4th DCA 2008), read the 2007 statute. A lease let a tenant cancel by paying one month's rent. The court found "no problem, statutory or otherwise" with it: "Nothing in the statute precludes a landlord and tenant from agreeing in advance about the circumstances when a tenant may get out of the lease" (at 560). This cuts against you: Section 12.1 looks like such a clause, so the fee may not need an addendum. The same case struck a lease's 3-months'-rent charge for tenants who leave early, because 83.595 sets "the total universe of choices" for a landlord (at 560).
- Wilson v. Terwillinger, 140 So. 3d 1122 (Fla. 5th DCA 2014), read the 2012 statute. A signed addendum with an amount for an early termination fee was enforceable even though the lease body said nothing; "landlords must obtain from the tenant an executed addendum to the lease agreement" (at 1124). That matters only if you signed one, which is not known yet.
- Mansur v. Eubanks, 401 So. 2d 1328 (Fla. 1981), Bennett v. Mattison, 382 So. 2d 873 (Fla. 1st DCA 1980), Paterson v. Deeb, 472 So. 2d 1210 (Fla. 1st DCA 1985), Bennett M. Lifter, Inc. v. Varnado, 480 So. 2d 1336 (Fla. 3d DCA 1985), Haynes v. Lloyd, 533 So. 2d 944 (Fla. 5th DCA 1988), Ray v. Tampa Windridge Associates, 596 So. 2d 676 (Fla. 2d DCA 1991), Menendez v. Palms West Condo. Ass'n, 736 So. 2d 58 (Fla. 1st DCA 1999), and Smith v. Grove Apartments, LLC, 976 So. 2d 582 (Fla. 3d DCA 2007) are tenants' injury suits (a gas explosion, falls, an attack, a scalding). None is about ending a lease. Mansur says a landlord has "a continuing duty to exercise reasonable care to repair dangerous defective conditions upon notice of their existence by the tenant" (at 1330). Paterson says a violation of the act is "at least evidence of negligence" (at 1216). Those would matter only if you were hurt and sued. Haynes (at 945) found the common-area section "not particularly relevant" there, which cuts against leaning on 83.51(2)(a) for the hallway leak.
- Solomon v. Gentry, 388 So. 2d 52 (Fla. 4th DCA 1980), read the 1979 statute. A tenant's home burned after a heater was repaired. The court held "no such warranty arises under a lease of real property" (at 53). It cuts against any claim that the unit is simply unfit without the statute's notice steps.

content:
Short version first. The tool cannot give you a plain yes or no on leaving, because the answer turns on two points the statute does not settle. Here is what it can say.

Can you leave? Ending the lease over the repair is not settled (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). The steps are done: you gave the written notice, and the program's deadlines show the 7 days have passed. Your lease promises the AC repair (Lease Section 7.1). If the two open points go your way, the statute says you "may terminate the rental agreement." If one does not, that way out is closed. The two points are whether paying October rent waived it, and whether the problem counts as "material."

Is "closed" on the fee route good or bad? It does not mean you cannot leave. It means one route is shut: the fee under Fla. Stat. 83.595(4), which is available "only if" you signed "a separate addendum to the rental agreement" when the lease was made. If you signed none, the landlord cannot charge a fee under that section. That is good for you on the fee. Whether you signed one is not confirmed yet. You said you do not remember signing one; the sheet after this asks you. Your mom's guaranty is a separate paper (Lease Section 4.3). What it says is in that paper, which the tool has not read.
Two limits on that. First, "closed" does not mean you owe nothing. When a tenant leaves, the landlord may choose among the remedies in 83.595, including "holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(3)). The tool cannot say which one the landlord would pick or give one amount. Second, your lease has its own early termination option with a fee of $1,578.00 (Lease Section 12.1). Olen Properties Corp. v. Moss, 984 So. 2d 558 (Fla. 4th DCA 2008), printed above, says "Nothing in the statute precludes a landlord and tenant from agreeing in advance about the circumstances when a tenant may get out of the lease" (at 560). That cuts against you. Whether the fee under Section 12.1 could be charged with no addendum is not settled here.

Did paying October rent hurt? It may have. The statute speaks of a tenant who "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). Those words are about knowing the problem, and you confirmed you knew of it when you paid. The same sentence says the waiver does not reach "any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." The statute does not settle which applies to a problem that is still not fixed. One reading: it is a continuing noncompliance, so paying did not waive ending the lease. Other reading: the failure to fix a problem you already knew of is the noncompliance, so paying did waive it, and only a new or different failure starts over.

What each option needs first, so you can choose:
- Ending the lease over the repair: no new step from the statute, since the notice and the 7 days are done. The open points are for a court to settle, not something you can fix tomorrow.
- Stopping rent over the problem: not known yet. It needs a code that covers the problem (Fla. Stat. 83.51(1)(a)). The city or county code enforcement office can tell you whether one does, and can inspect the unit. If one does, you would then need a new written notice saying you intend not to pay rent because of it, and 7 days (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). Send it as your lease says: by hand to the leasing office, by certified mail, or by e-mail to office@magnoliarow.example (Lease Section 13.1).
- The fee route: look through your move-in papers for any separate page about an early termination fee or liquidated damages.
- Leaving: your lease asks for 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery before you vacate, or you "shall forfeit the security deposit" (Lease Section 9.2; Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The sheet asks for your move-out date.

args.topic: Landlord's remedies after a tenant's breach

content:
The fee. You confirmed you signed no separate addendum, so the fee route in the statute is closed (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). That is good for you: the landlord cannot charge a fee under that section. It does not settle the $1,578.00 in your lease, which is the price of the lease's own early termination option, with 60 days' written notice (Lease Section 12.1). Olen Properties Corp. v. Moss, 984 So. 2d 558 (Fla. 4th DCA 2008), read the 2007 statute. The court said "Nothing in the statute precludes a landlord and tenant from agreeing in advance about the circumstances when a tenant may get out of the lease" (at 560). That cuts against you. It differs from yours: it was a challenge to lease clauses, not a tenant leaving over repairs. The same case struck a lease's 3-months'-rent charge, because 83.595 is "the total universe of choices" for a landlord (at 560). Whether Section 12.1's fee can be charged with no addendum is not settled.

"Rent as it comes due." Leaving does not by itself mean you owe all the rent. When a tenant leaves, the choice is the landlord's: end the lease and your liability (Fla. Stat. 83.595(1)); relet for your account, with "a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (83.595(2)); or "holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due" (83.595(3)). The third is the one that keeps you on the rent. The tool cannot say which the landlord would pick, and it does not work out an amount, so it cannot confirm your $7,000 figure.
Atlantis Estate Acquisitions, Inc. v. DePierro, 125 So. 3d 889 (Fla. 4th DCA 2013): the landlord ended the lease, and the court held "Termination under the first option also ends any further liability of the tenant under the rental agreement" (at 892). It also noted the landlord "did not make the tenant aware that it would hold the tenant liable for continuing obligations under the lease" (at 893). That helps you if the landlord ends the lease. It differs because there the landlord had acted, and yours has not yet. Olen also says that where a landlord cannot relet, "the ability to recover actual damages benefits the landlord" (at 561), and 83.55 says an aggrieved party "may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.55). Those cut against you.
Ending the lease over the repair (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)) is still not settled, for the two reasons before. If it holds, the lease ends. The tool does not work out what, if anything, is owed after that.
Your mom: a bill to her turns on the guaranty she signed (Lease Section 4.3). The tool has not read it, so it cannot say what it covers. That paper is where you can check.

One change from the move-out date you gave: the program's deadlines show the last day to give the 7-day notice before leaving has passed (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). Your lease says missing it means you "shall forfeit the security deposit" (Lease Section 9.2). The statute says missing it "does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit." That is about the deposit, not whether you can leave. The tool counts only from the date you confirmed.

The letter. It goes to the landlord named in Lease Section 1.1, sent as your lease says: "delivered by hand to the leasing office at 2600 SW Hartwell Lane, Gainesville, Florida 32608, sent by certified mail to that address, or sent by e-mail to office@magnoliarow.example" (Lease Section 13.1). I need these before I can draft it:
1. Which letter: about the repair, or about your leaving.
2. What you want the landlord to do.
3. How many days you give them to reply.
4. Which of those three ways you will send it.
5. Which posture. For the repair:
 preserve: "Describes the condition and asks for the repair. Cites nothing."
 assert: "Adds the 83.51(1) duty, quoted."
 escalate: "Adds the 83.56(1) sentence, quoted."
For your leaving:
 preserve: "States the planned move-out date and a forwarding address, and asks the landlord to confirm what, if anything, the landlord will charge. Cites nothing."
 assert: "Adds the 83.49(5) sentence on notice before vacating, quoted."
 escalate: "Adds the 83.595(4) sentence on liquidated damages or an early termination fee, quoted."
6. For a leaving letter, the address where you can be reached after you move.
A letter counts as the notice in 83.56(1) only if it states your intention to end the lease over the problem, and as the notice in 83.60(1)(b) only if it states your intention not to pay rent over it.

The deposit first.

Would leaving on that date lose it? Your lease says that if you vacate early without 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery, you "shall forfeit the security deposit" (Lease Section 9.2). The statute says missing that notice "does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). They differ. One statute makes a lease term void "to the extent that it" "purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part" (Fla. Stat. 83.47(1)(a)). But 83.49(5) itself opens with "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement." The text I have does not settle whether Section 9.2's forfeiture is such a term or is void. So the tool cannot say you would lose it, and cannot say you would keep it. The deposit is $300.00 (Lease Section 4.1). This notice is about the deposit only. It does not change whether you can end the lease, the fee, or the rent.

Should you move out a few days later? That is your choice, and the tool cannot count it for you. It counts the 7 days back from the move-out date you confirmed, and from any other date it computes nothing. If you settle on a new date, tell me, the sheet will ask you to confirm it, and the program's deadlines will then show whether the last day has passed. The notice must go by certified mail or personal delivery and include the address where you can be reached (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). E-mail is not named there or in Lease Section 9.2, so the by-hand delivery is the one that counts. Keep proof of the day you hand it in. The tool cannot weigh $300 against your health. That is yours to decide.

The letter, about your leaving. I have your reasons (the AC, the mold, and your asthma), what you ask for (to be let out of the lease with no fee, no charge to you or your mom for the rest of the rent, and your deposit back), 3 days to reply, by hand to the leasing office and by e-mail, and your address after the move, 5120 Beach Blvd, Jacksonville FL 32207. I will put your reasons in what you ask for. The letter uses the move-out date on file, so confirm a new date first if you change it. What I still need is the posture. Here is each, word for word:
 preserve: "States the planned move-out date and a forwarding address, and asks the landlord to confirm what, if anything, the landlord will charge. Cites nothing."
 assert: "Adds the 83.49(5) sentence on notice before vacating, quoted."
 escalate: "Adds the 83.595(4) sentence on liquidated damages or an early termination fee, quoted."
The three differ only in what statute words the letter quotes. preserve quotes nothing. assert quotes the sentence of 83.49(5) that asks for 7 days' written notice before vacating, with an address. escalate quotes that and the sentence of 83.595(4) saying the fee remedy "is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee." The tool does not pick one for you. For any of the three, the letter is the 83.49(5) notice only if it is sent by hand or certified mail and gives your new address.
Which do you want: preserve, assert, or escalate?

Landlord's notice of claim on the deposit

content:
Sorry I skipped those. Here they are in plain words.

1. Does the letter count as your notice, or do you need something else?
On its words, yes, for ending the lease. The statute asks for a written notice that names the problem and says you intend to end the lease because of it (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). Your letter names the AC and the mold and says "I am ending my lease because the AC and the mold were not fixed after I told you." The statute lists "delivering a true copy" and e-mailing as ways to deliver it (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)), and your lease lists by hand and e-mail (Lease Section 13.1). So you do not need a separate paper for that.
Three limits. First, you already gave a notice earlier. You confirmed it named the problem and said you intend to end the lease, and the program's deadlines show its 7 days have passed. This letter would be a second one. Check whether your earlier e-mail named the mold. If it did not, this letter is the first written notice naming the mold, and the 7 days for the mold would run from when it is delivered (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). The program computes only from a notice date you confirmed. Second, the letter does not say you will stop paying rent, so it is not the notice for that option (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). Third, a good notice does not settle the two open points from before: whether paying rent waived ending the lease, and whether the problem is "material." Ending the lease over the repair is still not settled.
Cases: Lakeway Management Co. of Florida v. Stolowilsky, 527 So. 2d 950 (Fla. 3d DCA 1988), treated a written complaint as the condition before a tenant who left could argue constructive eviction (at 951). K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith, 445 So. 2d 1032 (Fla. 5th DCA 1984), said a tenant claiming lost value must comply with 83.56 (at 1037). Both printed above. Yours has a written complaint, so you are on the right side of both. Neither says a notice alone lets you leave.

2. What happens if you hand it in tomorrow and move out on the date on file?
The program's deadlines show the last day to give the 7-day notice before that move-out date has passed. The tool does not count the days itself. So a letter handed in tomorrow would be late for that date.
The $300: not settled. Your lease says you "shall forfeit the security deposit" (Lease Section 9.2). The statute says missing the notice "does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). One reading: the lease may set its own term, since 83.49(5) opens with "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement," so the deposit is lost. Other reading: a lease term that waives rights in this part is void "to the extent that it" does so (Fla. Stat. 83.47(1)(a)), so the statute's line governs and you keep your rights to the deposit. The text I have does not pick one.
Something worse than the $300? The lease says the deposit is what a missed notice costs (Lease Section 9.2). The text I have names no other result for it. Whether a missed notice is itself a further breach, that text does not answer. Separately, whether leaving breaks the lease turns on the repair route, which is not settled. If it holds, the lease ends (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). If it does not, you left before the term ended, and the landlord chooses among the remedies in 83.595, including "holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(3)). A late notice does not appear in 83.595.
Cases, all printed above, and they cut against you:
- Plakhov v. Serova, 126 So. 3d 1221 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012), read the 2009 statute. A tenant moved out early with no 7-day notice. The court held "the Landlord's obligation to provide this notice was excused by the Tenant's failure to give the seven-day notice" (at 1223), and the deposit went to reduce the rent the landlord was owed. The landlord won a judgment for the rent. Yours differs in that you gave written notice of the problem, but a missed 7-day notice can let a landlord apply the deposit without the claim notice.
- Durene v. Alcime, 448 So. 2d 1208 (Fla. 3d DCA 1984), Malagon v. Solari, 566 So. 2d 352 (Fla. 4th DCA 1990), and Casey v. Picinich, 573 So. 2d 76 (Fla. 4th DCA 1990), say a landlord who misses the 30-day claim notice loses the deposit as a set-off. Durene adds that "the landlord may have an independent action for damages" (at 1210). They would help you only if the landlord owed you that claim notice. Plakhov says it did not, where the tenant skipped the 7-day notice (it distinguished Durene on that ground, at 1223).
